statement: In randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines for many conditions (62 trials reported adverse events; parallel-group and crossover trials combined), cannabinoids at the highest dose each trial tested, compared with placebo or another medicine, increase short-term side effects (the review's authors word this as an association). Side effects were common in both groups: across the 29 trials with counts for any adverse event in the review's forest plot, 1,438 of 1,779 people on cannabinoids (about 81 in 100) and 1,058 of 1,710 on placebo or another medicine (about 62 in 100) had at least one (crude totals, editors' arithmetic; the review's table gives 3,714 patients for these trials). In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), the odds of any adverse event were 3.03 times higher (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%) and of leaving a trial because of adverse events 2.94 times (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients), with no difference in deaths (1.01, 0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients). Specific effects more frequent with cannabinoids included disorientation (OR 5.41, 2.61 to 11.19), dizziness (5.09, 4.10 to 6.32; 41 studies), euphoria (4.08, 2.18 to 7.64), confusion (4.03, 2.05 to 7.97), drowsiness (3.68, 2.24 to 6.01), dry mouth (3.50, 2.58 to 4.75), somnolence (2.83, 2.05 to 3.91), loss of balance (2.62, 1.12 to 6.13), hallucination (2.19, 1.02 to 4.68; 10 studies), nausea (2.08, 1.63 to 2.65), asthenia (2.03, 1.35 to 3.06), fatigue (2.00, 1.54 to 2.62), vomiting (1.67, 1.13 to 2.47) and diarrhoea (1.65, 1.04 to 2.62); depression, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis and seizures did not differ clearly, with wide intervals (psychosis 1.09, 0.07 to 16.35; 2 studies, 37 patients). Apart from the counts for any adverse event, the review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect; using the highest dose was the authors' choice of a worst case; and no study of long-term adverse events was found, even among non-randomized studies. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In short trials, side effects were common with both cannabis medicines and the comparison: about 81 in 100 people taking a cannabis medicine and 62 in 100 taking a dummy medicine (placebo) or another medicine had at least one. Cannabis medicines raised the odds of any side effect, and of stopping the trial because of one, about three times, and of a serious one 1.4 times. Disorientation, dizziness, feeling high, confusion, drowsiness and dry mouth were among the most increased; nausea and vomiting were also more common. Deaths did not differ. The review used the highest dose each trial gave, gave counts only for having any side effect, and found no studies of long-term harms.
population: Patients with a range of conditions (chemotherapy, HIV/AIDS, chronic pain, spasticity, sleep problems, psychosis and others) in randomized trials published up to April 2015
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials, at the highest dose each trial tested (mostly nabiximols, dronabinol and nabilone); doses are study conditions
comparator: Placebo or an active comparator medicine
outcome: Any, serious and treatment-stopping adverse events, deaths, and individual adverse events, in the short term
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (highest dose) against placebo or active comparator, all indications, parallel-group and crossover trials: any adverse event, crude totals in Figure 4 1,438/1,779 vs 1,058/1,710 (80.8% vs 61.9%, editors' arithmetic; 3,489 patients against 3,714 in Table 3), OR 3.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%); serious 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%); withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients); death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients); psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29; 8 studies); nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58; 10 studies). Individual events: disorientation 5.41 (2.61 to 11.19); dizziness 5.09 (4.10 to 6.32); euphoria 4.08 (2.18 to 7.64); confusion 4.03 (2.05 to 7.97); drowsiness 3.68 (2.24 to 6.01); dry mouth 3.50 (2.58 to 4.75); somnolence 2.83 (2.05 to 3.91); loss of balance 2.62 (1.12 to 6.13); hallucination 2.19 (1.02 to 4.68); nausea 2.08 (1.63 to 2.65); asthenia 2.03 (1.35 to 3.06); fatigue 2.00 (1.54 to 2.62); vomiting 1.67 (1.13 to 2.47); diarrhoea 1.65 (1.04 to 2.62). Not significant: depression 1.32 (0.87 to 2.01), anxiety 1.98 (0.73 to 5.35), paranoia 2.05 (0.42 to 10.10), psychosis 1.09 (0.07 to 16.35), seizures 0.91 (0.05 to 15.66), dyspnoea 0.83 (0.26 to 2.63). No absolute frequencies for individual events.

evidence.extracted: Adverse events were reported in 62 studies (127 reports); meta-regression and stratified analyses found no difference in the association with any adverse event by cannabinoid, design, indication, comparator or duration, so all were combined (highest dose; placebo or active comparator). Any adverse event OR 3.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80), 29 studies, 3714 patients, I2 31%; serious adverse events 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92), 34 studies, 3248 patients, I2 0%; withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96), 23 studies, 2755 patients; death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00), 5 studies, 929 patients; psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29), 8 studies; nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58), 10 studies. No study of long-term adverse events was found, even among lower levels of evidence.

evidence.extracted: Synthesis: studies grouped by indication, cannabinoid and outcome and pooled with random effects; one data set per trial, the dose most similar to the other trials for benefits and the highest dose for adverse events, which the authors describe as a worst case; primary efficacy analyses restricted to parallel-group trials, but adverse-event data from all conditions and both designs were combined, with design tested in meta-regression.

evidence.extracted: Risk of bias across the 79 trials (Cochrane tool): 4 low, 55 high, 20 unclear; the main source was incomplete outcome data, with more than half of trials reporting substantial withdrawals not adequately handled; 57% reported appropriate blinding of participants and 24% of outcome assessors.

risk_of_bias.note: 55 of the 79 trials at high risk of bias, with substantial withdrawals often not handled (card sc_whiting_2015).

inconsistency.note: I2 31% and 0% for the main outcomes; meta-regression found no difference by cannabinoid, design, indication, comparator or duration.

indirectness.note: Worded for the highest dose, the short term and trial populations; typical doses and long-term use are not covered.

imprecision.note: Narrow intervals for the main outcomes; estimates for rare events such as psychosis or seizures are imprecise and are stated as unclear.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review, which used trial-registry records; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias: moderate for the short-term excess of adverse events as worded. The causal verb is the editors', used because the evidence is randomized and the certainty moderate; the review's authors word it as an association, and the review itself gives no GRADE rating for adverse events. Odds ratios overstate relative risks for common events: for any adverse event the crude totals are about 81 against 62 in 100, a ratio of about 1.3 (editors' arithmetic), against a pooled odds ratio of 3.03; no absolute frequencies are reported for individual events. Status replicated: 23 to 41 studies per main estimate, with low heterogeneity.
